title: Untangling the diversity of the South American native ungulates Adianthidae and Indaleciidae
content:
Abstract
South American native ungulates were extinct mammals that dominated South American ecosystems throughout much of the Cenozoic. Among them, the diverse Litopterna ranged from the early Palaeocene to the late Pleistocene and extended to Antarctic latitudes before the final breakup of Gondwana. Unlike Macraucheniidae, whose first representatives were discovered by Charles Darwin, or Proterotheriidae, which show strong convergence with equids, other litoptern families remain poorly known. The taxonomic placement of Adianthidae and Indaleciidae has long been unstable. They have been treated either as subfamilies (Adianthinae and Indaleciinae) within a single family (Adianthidae) or as members of separate orders (Litopterna and Notopterna). We analysed the hypodigms and identified the most derived indaleciid, Leindacia unpasajubo gen. et sp. nov., and a new adianthid, Dianthusa unlapla gen. et sp. nov., from the Oligocene and Miocene of Patagonia, respectively. Amilnedwardsiidae and Notonychopidae, both considered Litopterna or Notopterna, were also discussed. Our analysis indicates that the diversity of evolutionary experiments expressed in the dentition of litopterns greatly exceeds what is known in Macraucheniidae and Proterotheriidae. In particular, the new taxa share dental similarities, consistent with the hypothesis that adianthids may have occupied the ecological role of the extinct indaleciids in their ecological role in South America.
